samples.claim: committed_version=3 is the commit that made the overlay effective, not its read version. It is stamped at commit and restamped on retry. An index built at dataset_version >= committed_version incorporates the overlay; an older index must exclude affected cells for those fields and reevaluate current values. Greater committed_version wins across overlays; equal versions use later DataFragment.overlays position. Incorrect stamping or sorting changes query results.
samples.evidence:
222 |   /* The dataset version at which this overlay became effective: the version of
223 |    * the commit that introduced it, NOT the version it was read from. It is
224 |    * stamped at commit time and re-stamped if the commit is retried, in the same
225 |    * way as the created-at / last-updated-at version sequences.
226 |    *
227 |    * This drives two orderings:
228 |    *  * Versus index builds: an index whose `dataset_version` >= this value
229 |    *    already incorporates this overlay. Otherwise the overlay's covered cells
230 |    *    are excluded from index results for the affected fields and re-evaluated
231 |    *    against their current values (see the Data Overlay Files specification).
232 |    *  * Versus other overlays: when two overlays cover the same (offset, field),
233 |    *    the one with the higher `committed_version` wins. Overlays that share a
234 |    *    `committed_version` are ordered by their position in
235 |    *    `DataFragment.overlays`, where a later entry is newer and wins.
236 |    */
237 |   uint64 committed_version = 3;
238 | }

samples.claim: row_id_sequence holds serialized RowIdSequence bytes inline_row_ids=5, or an empty RowLineageColumn marker column_row_ids=12 referring to a file field -3. Row IDs follow physical row order, including unsorted example [1,42,3]. The comments say current writers keep inline bytes regardless of size. Any column arm requires manifest spilled-lineage flag 2048; otherwise an older reader could see an unset oneof and falsely infer no row IDs. This is a schema contract; current writer behavior still needs source confirmation.

38 |    * first row is row 1, the second row is row 42, and the third row is row 3.
39 |    */

41 |     // Current Lance writers store row ids inline regardless of encoded size.
42 |     bytes inline_row_ids = 5;
43 |     /* The row ids are a hidden column of one of this fragment's `files`: the
44 |      * entry whose `fields` carries the reserved id -3. See RowLineageColumn.

samples.claim: Optional materialization_readahead_bytes=13 is a nonzero byte bound on Blob v2 materialization reserved while awaiting ordered emission for one scanner execution. Optional batch_size_bytes=14 adds a byte boundary alongside row-based batch_size and corresponds to FileReaderOptions.batch_size_bytes. Neither option is a universal hard cap on all memory, and the schema itself cannot enforce nonzero values.

samples.claim: DataFile.path=1 is dataset-relative. fields=2 lists signed field IDs: in-memory -1 is unassigned and must not persist; -2 is tombstoned; all negatives are reserved system values rather than schema fields and projection skips them, including -3/-4/-5 lineage IDs. The v1 comment assigns IDs by file position plus existing maximum and counts nested struct/list fields but one ID for a fixed-size list; v1 IDs are sorted but need not be contiguous. For v2 the field ID cannot determine the physical column because encoding choices change column count, so use column_indices. The example's wording about second fragments versus files is retained as a comment-level account, not confirmed allocator behavior.
samples.evidence:
90 | message DataFile {
91 |   // Path to the root relative to the dataset's URI.
92 |   string path = 1;
93 |   /* The ids of the fields/columns in this file.
94 |    *
95 |    * When a DataFile object is created in memory, every value in fields is assigned -1 by
96 |    * default. An object with a value in fields of -1 must not be stored to disk. -2 is
97 |    * used for "tombstoned", meaning a field that is no longer in use. This is often
98 |    * because the original field id was reassigned to a different data file.
99 |    *
100 |    * Every negative value is reserved for system use and never names a field of the
101 |    * dataset schema. -3, -4 and -5 are the hidden row lineage columns (see
102 |    * RowLineageColumn); a reader projecting the dataset schema onto a file skips
103 |    * them, and any other negative value, rather than reject the file.
104 |    *
105 |    * In Lance v1 IDs are assigned based on position in the file, offset by the max
106 |    * existing field id in the table (if any already). So when a fragment is first created
107 |    * with one file of N columns, the field ids will be 1, 2, ..., N. If a second fragment
108 |    * is created with M columns, the field ids will be N+1, N+2, ..., N+M.
109 |    *
110 |    * In Lance v1 there is one field for each field in the input schema, this includes
111 |    * nested fields (both struct and list).  Fixed size list fields have only a single
112 |    * field id (these are not considered nested fields in Lance v1).
113 |    *
114 |    * This allows column indices to be calculated from field IDs and the input schema.
115 |    *
116 |    * In Lance v2 the field IDs generally follow the same pattern but there is no
117 |    * way to calculate the column index from the field ID.  This is because a given
118 |    * field could be encoded in many different ways, some of which occupy a different
119 |    * number of columns.  For example, a struct field could be encoded into N + 1 columns
120 |    * or it could be encoded into a single packed column.  To determine column indices
121 |    * the column_indices property should be used instead.
122 |    *
123 |    * In Lance v1 these ids must be sorted but might not always be contiguous.
124 |    */
125 |   repeated int32 fields = 2;

samples.claim: Stable persisted contracts preserve existing field numbers and backwards compatibility. Exclusively unstable schemas need not preserve earlier unstable revisions, but shared stable usage must be checked first. Execution-wire field numbers stay compatible unless all producers and consumers upgrade atomically.

13 | - Protobuf schemas that are part of a stable file format or any other stable persisted contract must remain backwards compatible. Never reuse or change their existing field numbers.
14 | - Protobuf schemas used exclusively by an unstable file format follow the root file-format stability contract: do not preserve compatibility with prior unstable revisions. Before making a breaking protobuf change, verify that the schema is not shared with a stable format or another persisted contract.
15 | - Execution wire schemas may still cross process or version boundaries. Preserve their field-number compatibility unless all producers and consumers are upgraded atomically.

samples.claim: DeletionFile path is {root}/_deletions/{fragment_id}-{read_version}-{id}.{extension}. Nested DeletionFileType is ARROW_ARRAY=0 (one Arrow IPC batch containing one Int32Array column, .arrow) or BITMAP=1 (Roaring bitmap, .bin). Comments motivate sparse versus dense selection but provide no threshold. Fields are file_type=1, read_version=2, concurrent-writer differentiating id=3, num_deleted_rows=4, and optional base_id=7 for Manifest.base_paths. Deletions operate on offsets, not stable logical IDs.
